Getting started with polychoice

Benjamin E. Bagozzi

Source: vignettes/polychoice.Rmd
polychoice.Rmd

The problem

Many outcomes in the social sciences are unordered choices among several alternatives: a vote for one of several candidates or for none, a travel mode, a type of political action, a treaty design. The workhorse model is the multinomial logit (Theil 1969; McFadden 1974), which comes in two notations that polychoice treats as one model:

  • the multinomial logit of the wide layout, one row per case, with case-specific covariates whose coefficients differ by alternative (y ~ x1 + x2);
  • the conditional logit of the long layout, one row per case and alternative, with alternative-specific covariates whose coefficients are common to all alternatives (chosen ~ w | x, with id and alt).

Both are the same choice probability

P(yi=j)=aijexp⁡(Vij)∑kaikexp⁡(Vik),Vij=oij+xi′βj+wij′γ, P(y_i = j) = \frac{a_{ij} \exp(V_{ij})}{\sum_k a_{ik} \exp(V_{ik})}, \qquad V_{ij} = o_{ij} + x_i'\beta_j + w_{ij}'\gamma,

with aija_{ij} indicating whether alternative jj is available to case ii, βb=0\beta_b = 0 for the base alternative, and an offset oijo_{ij}.

The model’s convenience comes with the independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): the odds between any two alternatives do not depend on the others. polychoice provides the estimators that relax IIA (nested logit, heteroskedastic extreme value, multinomial probit, random intercepts), the baseline-inflated multinomial logit of Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) for a base alternative that mixes two kinds of cases, and the full battery of tests of IIA and of specification, all behind one interface. This vignette covers the interface; the companion vignettes cover the inflated model, the tests, and the models beyond IIA.

One interface, seven estimators

Function Model
mnl() multinomial / conditional logit
imnl() inflated multinomial logit (one or several inflated alternatives)
nlogit() two-level nested logit
hev() heteroskedastic extreme value
mnprobit() multinomial probit with a free covariance
remnl() multinomial logit with random alternative-specific intercepts
rologit() rank-ordered (exploded) logit for rankings

Every estimator takes the same arguments for the data layout (id, alt), the base alternative (ref), frequency weights, an offset, unit fixed effects (fe; not imnl(), whose split equation they leave identified only through the functional form, nor remnl(), whose unit effects are the random intercepts, nor rologit()), and standard errors (se: inverse observed information, outer product of the scores, robust, cluster-robust, or bootstrap), and returns an object of class "choicemodel" with the usual methods (summary, coef, vcov, predict, confint, logLik, update, simulate) plus broom tidiers and texreg / modelsummary support.

A first fit: the 2006 Pennsylvania state House vote

pa2006 holds the survey of Arceneaux and Kolodny (2009) after a field experiment in which an interest group endorsed the Democratic candidate by canvassing or by telephone. The outcome has four alternatives, with abstention as the base.

library(polychoice)
data(pa2006)
table(pa2006$vote)
#> 
#>          abstain         democrat republican_other      nonresponse 
#>              731              579              563              125
m <- mnl(vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + age + female + voted2004,
         data = pa2006)
summary(m)
#> Multinomial logit 
#> Call: mnl(formula = vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + 
#>     age + female + voted2004, data = pa2006)

The coefficient names are alternative:term: each non-base alternative has its own equation against abstention. rrr() reports relative risk ratios (exponentiated coefficients) with confidence intervals; summary() also shows the information criteria and the standard-error type.

head(rrr(m), 6)
#>                  term   block   rrr lower upper      z  p.value
#>  democrat:(Intercept) outcome 0.054 0.028 0.104 -8.847  < 2e-16
#>      democrat:canvass outcome 0.991 0.661 1.485 -0.045    0.964
#>        democrat:phone outcome 0.958 0.659 1.392 -0.225    0.822
#>     democrat:democrat outcome 2.157 1.622 2.867  5.289 1.23e-07
#>   democrat:republican outcome 0.309 0.220 0.435 -6.737 1.62e-11
#>          democrat:age outcome 1.027 1.020 1.035  7.558 4.09e-14

Predicted probabilities and first differences

predict() returns the probability of every alternative for the estimation rows or for newdata; type = "class" picks the most likely alternative.

head(predict(m), 3)
#>     abstain   democrat republican_other nonresponse
#> 1 0.5149576 0.05840060        0.3747743  0.05186757
#> 2 0.3988234 0.07973611        0.4620162  0.05942424
#> 3 0.2399238 0.11691714        0.5770150  0.06614410
nd <- data.frame(canvass = c(0, 1), phone = 0, democrat = 1, republican = 0, age = 45,
                 female = 1, voted2004 = 1)
predict(m, newdata = nd)
#>     abstain  democrat republican_other nonresponse
#> 1 0.3428170 0.5129521       0.09332101  0.05090984
#> 2 0.3315748 0.4915459       0.12760476  0.04927454

first_difference() is the quantity of interest most analyses report: the change in every alternative’s probability when one covariate moves between two values. By default in the wide layout the other covariates are held at a profile of their weighted means and modes; newdata gives another one-case profile; average = TRUE (the default in the long layout) averages the first difference over the estimation cases, the average effect many applied reports prefer to the effect at a profile. The columns from and to are the two predicted probabilities. Delta-method intervals are the default; ci = "sim" draws from the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates instead.

first_difference(m, "canvass", from = 0, to = 1)
#> First differences: canvass from 0 to 1 at the covariate profile (delta intervals at 95%)
#>       alternative  from    to   diff  lower upper
#>           abstain 0.423 0.385 -0.038 -0.118 0.041
#>          democrat 0.271 0.244 -0.027 -0.096 0.042
#>  republican_other 0.248 0.318  0.071 -0.006 0.147
#>       nonresponse 0.058 0.053 -0.005 -0.038 0.028
first_difference(m, "canvass", from = 0, to = 1, average = TRUE)
#> First differences: canvass from 0 to 1, averaged over the estimation cases (delta intervals at 95%)
#>       alternative  from    to   diff  lower upper
#>           abstain 0.375 0.344 -0.031 -0.096 0.033
#>          democrat 0.296 0.275 -0.022 -0.081 0.037
#>  republican_other 0.264 0.324  0.059 -0.004 0.123
#>       nonresponse 0.064 0.058 -0.006 -0.041 0.028

Fit and classification

fit_stats() gives the log-likelihood, information criteria, and the pseudo-R2R^2 measures in common use (all relative to the null model with alternative-specific constants only); classification() cross-tabulates the observed and predicted alternatives.

fit_stats(m)
#> Log-likelihood -2125.695 (null -2511.718), 24 parameters, 1998 cases; AIC 4299.390, BIC 4433.788
#> McFadden R2 0.154 (adjusted 0.144); Cox-Snell 0.321; Nagelkerke 0.349
#> Count R2 0.553 (adjusted: 0.295 proportional reduction in error over the modal alternative)
classification(m)
#>                   predicted
#> observed           abstain democrat republican_other nonresponse
#>   abstain              365      194              172           0
#>   democrat             101      402               76           0
#>   republican_other     109      116              338           0
#>   nonresponse           41       54               30           0
#> 
#> Correctly classified: 0.553; proportional reduction in error over the modal alternative: 0.295

The long layout: alternative-specific covariates

When covariates vary across alternatives (travel time, price, distance to a polling place), the data come as one row per case and alternative and the formula has two parts: chosen ~ w | x, where w are the alternative-specific covariates with a common coefficient and x the case-specific ones with alternative-specific coefficients. The intercept of the first part switches the alternative-specific constants on (the default); chosen ~ 0 + w | x switches them off. The classic example is the Australian travel mode data distributed with the AER package.

data("TravelMode", package = "AER")
TM <- TravelMode
TM$chosen <- as.integer(TM$choice == "yes")
head(TM, 4)
#>   individual  mode choice wait vcost travel gcost income size chosen
#> 1          1   air     no   69    59    100    70     35    1      0
#> 2          1 train     no   34    31    372    71     35    1      0
#> 3          1   bus     no   35    25    417    70     35    1      0
#> 4          1   car    yes    0    10    180    30     35    1      1
mc <- mnl(chosen ~ wait + vcost + travel + gcost | income + size, data = TM,
          id = "individual", alt = "mode")
summary(mc)
#> Conditional logit 
#> Call: mnl(formula = chosen ~ wait + vcost + travel + gcost | income + 
#>     size, data = TM, id = "individual", alt = "mode")
#> Alternatives: air, train, bus, car  (base: air)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>                    Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> train:(Intercept)  0.421795   1.073173   0.393   0.6943    
#> train:income      -0.067576   0.016455  -4.107 4.01e-05 ***
#> train:size         0.693524   0.378587   1.832   0.0670 .  
#> bus:(Intercept)   -0.570171   1.210541  -0.471   0.6376    
#> bus:income        -0.028019   0.017093  -1.639   0.1012    
#> bus:size           0.290801   0.465637   0.625   0.5323    
#> car:(Intercept)   -5.286500   1.202630  -4.396 1.10e-05 ***
#> car:income        -0.008078   0.013419  -0.602   0.5472    
#> car:size           0.530701   0.321034   1.653   0.0983 .  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Generic coefficients (alternative-specific covariates):
#>         Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> wait   -0.102555   0.011376  -9.015  < 2e-16 ***
#> vcost  -0.053353   0.025282  -2.110  0.03484 *  
#> travel -0.010250   0.003418  -2.999  0.00271 ** 
#> gcost   0.046426   0.024900   1.865  0.06225 .  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -170.688 on 13 parameters, 210 cases. AIC 367.38, BIC 410.89.

A covariate in the first part can be given an alternative-specific coefficient with w:alt (for example vcost:mode, a cost coefficient per mode), so no third formula part is needed. Alternatives absent from a case’s rows are treated as unavailable to that case. This is also how a stated consideration set enters: when a survey asks which parties a respondent would consider voting for, keeping only those parties’ rows makes mnl() the model of the choice within the considered set (which parties are considered is then a separate set of binary models; Oscarsson and Rosema 2019 recommend such direct measures). A consideration set inferred from the choices alone, without such a question, is weakly identified in the designs political scientists have: the package’s verification found the standard errors of the consideration parameters as large as the parameters at 2,000 cases with respondent characteristics alone, recovery failing when the same voter-party distances drive both stages, and, even with a distance that shapes consideration only, intervals that covered 0.88-0.91 instead of 0.95 in a realistic design. The package does not fit it.

Rankings

When respondents rank the alternatives instead of choosing one (a survey that asks voters to order the parties, the ballots of a ranked-choice election), rologit() fits the rank-ordered logit (Beggs, Cardell and Hausman 1981), also called the exploded logit after Chapman and Staelin’s (1982) “explosion” of a ranking into independent choices. A ranking is read as a sequence of multinomial-logit choices: the first-ranked alternative from the whole choice set, the second from those left, and so on. Partial rankings (only the first few positions) and tied ranks are handled exactly (Allison and Christakis 1994). The data are in the long layout with the rank as the response, smaller preferred and 0 for an alternative left unranked; rrologit() simulates such data.

set.seed(8)
dk <- rrologit(800, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5), d = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.3)),
               gamma = 0.7, depth = 3)
head(dk, 4)
#>   id alt rank         w1          x1       x2
#> 1  1   a    2  0.9824732 -0.08458607 0.492746
#> 2  1   b    1 -0.4606749 -0.08458607 0.492746
#> 3  1   c    3  0.7402164 -0.08458607 0.492746
#> 4  1   d    0 -0.4267571 -0.08458607 0.492746
mro <- rologit(rank ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dk, id = "id", alt = "alt")
mfc <- rologit(rank ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = dk, id = "id", alt = "alt", depth = 1)   # first choices only
cbind(rankings = sqrt(diag(vcov(mro))), first_choices = sqrt(diag(vcov(mfc))))[c(1:3, 10), ]
#>                 rankings first_choices
#> b:(Intercept) 0.07348825    0.11778461
#> b:x1          0.08144944    0.12364952
#> b:x2          0.08078852    0.12496424
#> w1            0.03324162    0.05316619

The rankings estimate the same coefficients as the first choices with smaller standard errors. The model assumes that preferences are the same at every stage of the ranking; rank_test() refits with separate coefficients for the stages after the first and tests the difference (Hausman and Ruud 1987, section 3; Allison and Christakis 1994, section 5.4):

rank_test(mro, after = 1)
#> Stability of preferences across ranking stages (position 1 against later; 800 ranking(s) with later stages) 
#>              test statistic df p.value
#>  Likelihood ratio    17.721 10  0.0599
#>              Wald    17.659 10  0.0610

Standard errors, weights, and panels

se = "robust" gives the sandwich over cases; cluster = "<cluster column>" the cluster-robust version (and selects se = "cluster"); se = "bootstrap" resamples cases, or clusters when cluster is given (units with unit fixed effects or random intercepts), with nboot refits. weights are frequency weights: a case with weight 2 counts as two identical cases in the estimates, the model-based standard errors, the information criteria, and the averaged quantities of interest. Survey (probability) weights are not supported: se = "robust" is the frequency-weight sandwich, not a design-based variance (see ?mnl).

mr <- mnl(vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + age + female + voted2004,
          data = pa2006, se = "robust")
cbind(analytic = sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[1:4], robust = sqrt(diag(vcov(mr)))[1:4])
#>                       analytic    robust
#> democrat:(Intercept) 0.3292465 0.3296794
#> democrat:canvass     0.2063913 0.2053533
#> democrat:phone       0.1907265 0.1901162
#> democrat:democrat    0.1453229 0.1450103

For panels, fe = "<unit column>" (the name of the column that identifies the units) adds alternative-specific constants per unit (with the never-chosen rule and, optionally, bias_correct = "jackknife"), remnl() integrates out random alternative-specific intercepts, and mundlak() adds unit means of the covariates for a correlated random-effects specification. These are covered in the vignette Beyond IIA.

Reporting

broom::tidy() and broom::glance() work on every fit, and texreg and modelsummary tables can be built directly from the fitted objects.

head(broom::tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE), 4)
#>                   term     estimate std.error   statistic      p.value
#> 1 democrat:(Intercept) -2.912733973 0.3292465 -8.84666761 9.017146e-19
#> 2     democrat:canvass -0.009283797 0.2063913 -0.04498153 9.641220e-01
#> 3       democrat:phone -0.042843030 0.1907265 -0.22463074 8.222665e-01
#> 4    democrat:democrat  0.768583198 0.1453229  5.28879633 1.231239e-07
#>   component   conf.low  conf.high
#> 1   outcome -3.5580452 -2.2674228
#> 2   outcome -0.4138033  0.3952357
#> 3   outcome -0.4166601  0.3309740
#> 4   outcome  0.4837556  1.0534108
broom::glance(m)
#>      logLik     AIC      BIC df nobs converged boundary ill_conditioned
#> 1 -2125.695 4299.39 4433.788 24 1998      TRUE    FALSE           FALSE
#>   singular n_modes
#> 1    FALSE       1

With multiply imputed data, fit the model on each completed data set and pass the list of fits to mice::pool(), which combines them by Rubin’s rules through the same methods. The estimators take the data as an argument, so with(imp, mnl(...)) does not work. The fits’ flags are not pooled, so check each fit first. And give pool() the complete-data degrees of freedom, cases minus parameters: left to itself, mice 3.19 counts one residual per case and alternative. The pooled statistic tests each parameter against zero (?tidy.choicemodel).

set.seed(1)
dm <- rmnl(500, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5)))
dm$x1[sample(500, 80)] <- NA
imp <- mice::mice(dm, m = 5, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 1)
fits <- lapply(1:5, function(i) mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = mice::complete(imp, i)))
all(vapply(fits, function(f) f$converged && !f$boundary && !f$singular, logical(1)))
#> [1] TRUE
pooled <- mice::pool(fits, dfcom = nobs(fits[[1]]) - length(coef(fits[[1]])))
summary(pooled)[, c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "df", "p.value")]
#>            term   estimate std.error statistic        df      p.value
#> 1 b:(Intercept)  0.4821263 0.1232712  3.911103 475.78603 1.052452e-04
#> 2          b:x1 -0.7073566 0.1777954 -3.978486  31.11162 3.859728e-04
#> 3          b:x2  0.6748004 0.1309133  5.154561 441.90770 3.841501e-07
#> 4 c:(Intercept) -0.3711618 0.1679398 -2.210088 253.25992 2.799368e-02
#> 5          c:x1  0.9470919 0.1783153  5.311331 119.41062 5.113435e-07
#> 6          c:x2 -0.6314056 0.1471864 -4.289837 330.41730 2.350910e-05

Where next

  • The inflated multinomial logit fits the model of Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) and reproduces the published applications.
  • Testing IIA and specification covers iia_tests() and the further tests, with the size study that motivates the recommendations.
  • Beyond IIA covers the nested logit, HEV, multinomial probit, random intercepts, and the fixed-effects tools.
  • Seven published analyses works through the example datasets drawn from replication archives (sanctions, fluvax, bes1987, defection, bes2010, cabinets, afghan_leaders), four of them reproducing their published models, one of them with Firth’s penalized likelihood under separation.

References

Bagozzi, B.E. and Marchetti, K. (2017). Distinguishing occasional abstention from routine indifference in models of vote choice. Political Science Research and Methods, 5(2), 277-294.

Chapman, R.G. and Staelin, R. (1982). Exploiting rank ordered choice set data within the stochastic utility model. Journal of Marketing Research, 19, 288-301.

Hausman, J.A. and Ruud, P.A. (1987). Specifying and testing econometric models for rank-ordered data. Journal of Econometrics, 34, 83-104.

McFadden, D. (1974). Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behavior. In P. Zarembka (ed.), Frontiers in Econometrics, 105-142. Academic Press.
